# President Reagan challenges Gorbachev to “Tear down this wall”
HISTORY.com Editors
Wally McNamee/Corbis/Getty Images
Published: November 13, 2009 Last Updated: March 02, 2025
On June 12, 1987, in one of his most famous Cold War speeches, President Ronald Reagan challenges Soviet Leader Mikhail Gorbachev to “tear down” the Berlin Wall, a symbol of the repressive Communist era in a divided Germany.
In 1945, following Germany’s defeat in World War II, the nation’s capital, Berlin, was divided into four sections, with the Americans, British and French controlling the western region and the Soviets gaining power in the eastern region. In May 1949, the three western sections came together as the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany), with the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) being established in October of that same year. In 1952, the border between the two countries was closed and by the following year East Germans were prosecuted if they left their country without permission. In August 1961, the Berlin Wall was erected by the East German government to prevent its citizens from escaping to the West. Between 1949 and the wall’s inception, it’s estimated that over 2.5 million East Germans fled to the West in search of a less repressive life.

# President Reagan challenges Gorbachev to “Tear down this wall”
## Here's How the Truman Doctrine Established the Cold War
Learn how the Truman Doctrine marked the beginning of the Cold War, how it shaped America's attitude towards communism and how it shifted its foreign policy on interventionism with its involvement in the Mediterranean after World War II.
4:46m watch
With the wall as a backdrop, President Reagan declared to a West Berlin crowd in 1987, “There is one sign the Soviets can make that would be unmistakable, that would advance dramatically the cause of freedom and peace.” He then called upon his Soviet counterpart: “Secretary General Gorbachev, if you seek peace—if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe—if you seek liberalization: come here, to this gate. Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate. Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.” Reagan then went on to ask Gorbachev to undertake serious arms reduction talks with the United States.
Most listeners at the time viewed Reagan’s speech as a dramatic appeal to Gorbachev to renew negotiations on nuclear arms reductions. It was also a reminder that despite the Soviet leader’s public statements about a new relationship with the West, the U.S. wanted to see action taken to lessen Cold War tensions. Happily for Berliners, though, the speech also foreshadowed events to come: Two years later, on November 9, 1989, joyful East and West Germans did break down the infamous barrier between East and West Berlin. Germany was officially reunited on October 3, 1990.
Gorbachev, who had been in office since 1985, stepped down from his post as Soviet leader in 1991. Reagan, who served two terms as president, from 1981 to 1989, died on June 5, 2004, at age 93.Gorbachev died on August 30, 2022, at age 91.

Title: The Last Flight To Berlin
Chunks: 0,1,2
In November of 1989, I was traveling from North Africa to Frankfurt, Germany, when I read about the protests at the Berlin Wall and the possibility of, well, no one was quite sure what the possibilities were. When I heard what was happening, I immediately changed my plans and hopped on the last plane from Frankfurt to Berlin that night. A colleague met me at the airport, and we sped into town to the location near the wall where crowds were gathering. Parking blocks away, I grabbed my camera bag, and we jumped out of the car and ran. Still blocks away, before we could see anything, we could hear the roar. Like nothing I had ever heard. What popped into my mind was the loud swell at a Super Bowl when the crowd cheered a phenomenal play.
Pink Floyd’s “The Wall” blasted over loudspeakers. We stopped at the edge of the large plaza and surveyed the scene before us. It was surreal. Two huge spotlights illuminated the wall and some of the crowd. The “stage” was lit. People of all ages were dancing, hugging, and toasting with bottles of champagne. The November air was crisp, and you could see people’s breath. I turned around and saw ABC News anchor Peter Jennings there, as well as CBS anchor Dan Rather.
As we moved through the crowd to get closer to the wall, we could feel the spray of a champagne bottle being opened. I wanted to get close to the wall to photograph the people on top, some standing, some sitting. People, mostly young adults, were on top of the wall hammering and chiseling away, chipping off pieces of the wall, cheering and waving West German flags. Others were being hoisted up on shoulders so they could perch on the wall. I don’t remember seeing any East German guards on top of the wall that night.
When I arrived that night, with the crowds cheering all around me, I knew history was being made. Standing in front of the wall, I felt a sea change, the beginning of the end of the Cold War that had been in effect all my life. Russia was unknown, a mystery to me. The people behind the wall were almost ghosts. Berlin was the setting for spy novels, pitting the Western way of life against the East.

This photograph was taken the next day as expectations built and no one knew quite what was going to happen. The city of Berlin was restless. The man in the fedora on the right seems as if from another era, and the man on the left seems to be peering at something or someone above and to my left. The young East German guards are quiet, watching. The wall has gaps in places from the chiseling the night before. People were milling about with an air of expectation.
The Berlin Wall was erected in the dead of night on August 12–13, 1961, as soldiers and construction workers tore up streets, put up concrete posts, and strung barbed wire all across the border between East and West Berlin, officially closing off the symbolic boundary between East and West Germany. As historian Jennifer Rosenberg wrote, “whichever side of the border one went to sleep on during the night of August 12, they were stuck on that side for decades.” In 1963, President John F. Kennedy stood in Berlin and said, “Ich bin ein Berliner.” In 1987, President Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate and said, “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.” Reagan was speaking more to Gorbachev than to Berliners, and it wasn’t until after November 1989 that his speech came to be seen as iconic.
I grew up with a vision of a real “Iron Curtain.” When I was young, I thought there was a structural iron curtain separating Eastern Europe from the West. The phrase “iron curtain” was coined by Winston Churchill in a 1946 speech: “From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.” I grew up with whispers of communism and the horrors that went on in Russia and the Eastern Bloc countries: children turned against parents, the grocery stores were bare, and the secret police watched everything you did. When someone “defected,” it was cause for celebration. In elementary school, we had air raid tests where we either had to hide under our desks or file out into the hall and sit on the floor, waiting out fate. The Soviet Union was a mysterious giant looming large in our imaginations. The Berlin Wall was monumental. It, too, was shrouded in mystery.

The next day we went to the Glienicke Bridge, where during the Cold War, spies were exchanged. It looked just like the movies: a cold, dreary November day.
I thought of the man in the fedora I had seen earlier that day.

In November of 1989, I was traveling from North Africa to Frankfurt, Germany, when I read about the protests at the Berlin Wall and the possibility of, well, no one was quite sure what the possibilities were. When I heard what was happening, I immediately changed my plans and hopped on the last plane from Frankfurt to Berlin that night. A colleague met me at the airport, and we sped into town to the location near the wall where crowds were gathering. Parking blocks away, I grabbed my camera bag, and we jumped out of the car and ran. Still blocks away, before we could see anything, we could hear the roar. Like nothing I had ever heard. What popped into my mind was the loud swell at a Super Bowl when the crowd cheered a phenomenal play.
Pink Floyd’s “The Wall” blasted over loudspeakers. We stopped at the edge of the large plaza and surveyed the scene before us. It was surreal. Two huge spotlights illuminated the wall and some of the crowd. The “stage” was lit. People of all ages were dancing, hugging, and toasting with bottles of champagne. The November air was crisp, and you could see people’s breath. I turned around and saw ABC News anchor Peter Jennings there, as well as CBS anchor Dan Rather.
As we moved through the crowd to get closer to the wall, we could feel the spray of a champagne bottle being opened. I wanted to get close to the wall to photograph the people on top, some standing, some sitting. People, mostly young adults, were on top of the wall hammering and chiseling away, chipping off pieces of the wall, cheering and waving West German flags. Others were being hoisted up on shoulders so they could perch on the wall. I don’t remember seeing any East German guards on top of the wall that night.
When I arrived that night, with the crowds cheering all around me, I knew history was being made. Standing in front of the wall, I felt a sea change, the beginning of the end of the Cold War that had been in effect all my life. Russia was unknown, a mystery to me. The people behind the wall were almost ghosts. Berlin was the setting for spy novels, pitting the Western way of life against the East.

This photograph was taken the next day as expectations built and no one knew quite what was going to happen. The city of Berlin was restless. The man in the fedora on the right seems as if from another era, and the man on the left seems to be peering at something or someone above and to my left. The young East German guards are quiet, watching. The wall has gaps in places from the chiseling the night before. People were milling about with an air of expectation.
The Berlin Wall was erected in the dead of night on August 12–13, 1961, as soldiers and construction workers tore up streets, put up concrete posts, and strung barbed wire all across the border between East and West Berlin, officially closing off the symbolic boundary between East and West Germany. As historian Jennifer Rosenberg wrote, “whichever side of the border one went to sleep on during the night of August 12, they were stuck on that side for decades.” In 1963, President John F. Kennedy stood in Berlin and said, “Ich bin ein Berliner.” In 1987, President Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate and said, “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.” Reagan was speaking more to Gorbachev than to Berliners, and it wasn’t until after November 1989 that his speech came to be seen as iconic.
I grew up with a vision of a real “Iron Curtain.” When I was young, I thought there was a structural iron curtain separating Eastern Europe from the West. The phrase “iron curtain” was coined by Winston Churchill in a 1946 speech: “From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.” I grew up with whispers of communism and the horrors that went on in Russia and the Eastern Bloc countries: children turned against parents, the grocery stores were bare, and the secret police watched everything you did. When someone “defected,” it was cause for celebration. In elementary school, we had air raid tests where we either had to hide under our desks or file out into the hall and sit on the floor, waiting out fate. The Soviet Union was a mysterious giant looming large in our imaginations. The Berlin Wall was monumental. It, too, was shrouded in mystery.

The next day we went to the Glienicke Bridge, where during the Cold War, spies were exchanged. It looked just like the movies: a cold, dreary November day.
I thought of the man in the fedora I had seen earlier that day.
